blocks.text: DR DEWI EVANS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by Mr Johnson
Welcome back, Dr Evans. For the record would you identify yourself, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Dewi Evans.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you, doctor. Relating to the case of [Baby H], if we may, you have written several reports; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Can we just identify those to start with, please. Was your original sift report 16 November 2017?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Your more substantive report, 31 May 2018?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you deal with identifying the specific records in a statement made on 24 June 2021?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Then ultimately, and most recently, did you deal with a few issues that had arisen in a report dated 20 October 2021?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. What I'd like to do, if we may, is concentrate on your report of 31 May 2018.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There, did you record [Baby H]'s details such as her name, her date of birth, her birth weight, her gestational age at birth?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Of all the cases that you considered was this the 12th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If look at your reference, which is "12 [Surname of Baby H]".
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it was, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So far as the material that you considered was concerned, did you receive medical records from both the Countess of Chester Hospital and from Arrowe Park on the Wirral?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did the Chester records include quite a few X-rays or radiographs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Just to put us in mind of what the chronology was, and I'm looking at your paragraph 6, did you record [Baby H]'s delivery by caesarean section at 18.22 hours on 22 September 2015?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Her birth weight at 2.33 kilos?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And her gestational age as 34 plus 4?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: From your examination of the records did it appear that [Baby H] had been born in good condition?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But that there were complications which were of note so far as the medics were concerned, not least the fact that [Baby H]'s mother had type 1 diabetes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you record the fact that [Baby H] was transferred to the neonatal unit because of her prematurity?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And that within 23 minutes of her birth, [Baby H] was mildly grunting and there were signs of some subcostal recession?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I think you've told us before, on more than one occasion probably, that they are signs of potential breathing problems?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, they are. These are early signs of a condition called respiratory distress syndrome, RDS, and RDS or respiratory distress syndrome is a common condition in premature babies and is due to the fact that the lungs have not matured satisfactorily to allow normal exchange of oxygen, and this is because they're born before their time. So respiratory distress syndrome in the bad old days, a common condition with lots of complications and also a significant mortality, although that is no longer the case.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. So far as gas exchange is concerned, just to remind those of us for whom this is becoming a more distant memory, is that the mechanism that Dr Kinsey produced some diagrams to describe?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I think so, yes. It gives you an idea of the wellbeing of the baby because you need to know the carbon dioxide level because if the carbon dioxide level is high then the baby's respirations are not satisfactory and so that's the main reason for checking the blood gas level at this juncture.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you note at your paragraph 9 that by 10.50 in the morning of the following day, 23 September, [Baby H] was on CPAP and requiring a relatively low but additional rate of oxygen at 26%?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. 26% oxygen is quite a low figure. The standard management of RDS initially is additional oxygen, of course, and also this condition of CPAP, continuous positive airways pressure, where you apply a mechanism to the baby's nose to allow -- to ensure that the baby's lungs do not wholly collapse following each breath.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So CPAP in mild RDS is sufficient management.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There's just a matter of law I'd like to raise, please, my Lord. I'm sorry.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, you'll remember I said at the very outset of the case, if an issue of law arises then I have to deal with it in your absence. You have to leave the courtroom at this stage because I deal with all the law, you deal with the facts.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
Should the witness withdraw?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There's no problem with the witness being here, my Lord. It's something that I didn't see and your Lordship's not well placed to see, but I'm told that the recently bereaved juror appears to be upset and isn't concentrating.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Oh right, sorry. I couldn't see that because she's behind a screen from my line of vision.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: She is crying, apparently.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What I shall do, unless anyone suggests otherwise, is ask the usher just to speak to her and say is she...
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm told she sort of pulled herself together by the time they were walking out.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: All right. Look, could you just discreetly and sensitively enquire of her if she is all right to proceed? You may have something you want to tell me.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
When I say discreetly -- yes. Thank you. It's not an easy situation, but I don't want there to be any further upset caused.
(Pause)
It may have been triggered by my reference to Monday and Tuesday.
Yes. This may make it worse again, that's the problem.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Pause)
There's no problem.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Good.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
Sorry about that. We're in a position to continue now.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right, Dr Evans, we'd just dealt with the position at 10.50 in the morning of 23 September, so day 2 for [Baby H].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On day 3, which is 24 September, is it right that [Baby H] was intubated at shortly after midnight, so 00.10?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. This is correct. The natural history of this condition called RDS is that CPAP isn't always effective and if the baby becomes worse, becomes less well, then you need to place the baby on ventilatory support. In other words, this is the procedure where you pass a tube into the trachea, into the lungs, and place a baby onto a breathing machine. So that took place and this is -- occurs in lots of babies who have RDS.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. But so far as -- so [Baby H] was being mechanically ventilated, but so far as the concentration of oxygen was concerned, having been at 26% on CPAP, what was the position with regard to the mechanical ventilation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, she initially required an increase in oxygen to 60%, but that improved after she was given surfactant.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, surfactant is this substance that has improved the outcome significantly with this condition and it's a substance that you place down the endotracheal tube, so it goes directly into the lungs and improves lung flexibility, so the lungs are able to breathe in and out much more effectively.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So she received surfactant and the other thing they did was they checked to rule out the possibility of a pneumothorax. We've had a lot of discussion about pneumothorax with this case, so I won't put any detail about that. But later, she was found to have reduced air entry on the left lung and on that occasion she was found to have a pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. What time was that, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That was at 08.58 hours on 24 September. So she's now -this is -- she was born on the 22nd, so it's day 3. So she's not quite 72 hours old yet.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: A pneumothorax is a life-threatening condition, untreated, because what it means is that you have sustained a puncture, effectively, of the lung somewhere and air has leaked from the lung into what we call the pleural space. The pleural space is the area between the outside of the lung and the inside of the chest wall.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Normally, the lung -- the outside of the lung fits snugly to the inside of the chest wall. There isn't a gap between the two. But with a pneumothorax, this leak leads to air getting into that space, this pleural space, and with each breath, if it's not treated, the amount of air increases and increases.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: This, of course, leads to several complications.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The first, of course, is that as you get more air into the pleural space, it's more difficult for the lung, the left lung, to expand. So therefore the lung collapses on itself, cannot expand normally. As the air continues to increase, you develop what's called tension or high pressure within this space, and that interferes not only with the ability of the lung to expand, it also pushes the heart, you know, which is in the middle of the chest, pushes the heart over to the other side and, on top of that, because you've got very high pressure due to pneumothorax in the lung, this interferes with the return of blood to the heart and this is a life-threatening phenomenon which demands urgent treatment. In other words, you need to treat the pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you then in your review refer to the fact that following the treatment which was offered for that condition, [Baby H] progressed through -- unremarkably, essentially -until the early hours of the morning of 25 September, when her ET tube was removed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Was that tube at that time found to be blocked by what you have termed as a mucus plug?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If the jury want a reference for that event in the sequence, that's at tile 152; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can I...?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's all right, I'm just giving them a reference for that event. All right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Now, following that, and I'm going to your paragraph 13, please, Dr Evans, did you note that there had been a crash call -- and we're at tile 243 if the jury want to follow it on the iPads -a crash call at 03.24 hours in the morning of 26 September?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Yes, there had been complications from the pneumothorax before then, but this was a crash call where -- and I've written -- I've quoted the entry at -- noting that this had occurred despite the fact that [Baby H] was not being handled.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There was no trigger, in other words it was not clear or obvious why she should have deteriorated so strikingly, and she required quite significant resuscitation with CPR and adrenaline and atropine. This was not the result of the pneumothorax recurring, which had occurred earlier, because they did a needle aspiration, which we've heard earlier in this case.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Is this the thoracocentesis?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thoracocentesis, yes. And they just drained 8ml of air and 2ml of fluid. Previously they'd drained far more than that. So 8ml of air would be insufficient to cause, you know, the very striking deterioration in her condition, where she had desaturated, with oxygen, to 60%.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So just putting this into the context of the evidence that we heard over the last couple of days -- and this is what was described to us by Dr Ventress; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Yes, because what my paragraph 13 also says is that the previous day she'd had 85ml of air aspirated from the chest at around 03.30 hours on the 25th.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Now, that's a lot of air and if you have -- sorry, if you have 85ml of air in your pleural cavity that is sufficient explanation for why your condition would have deteriorated. This is what led to them -- this is what led to her requiring another chest drain.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes, all right. Just to contextualise this, the event, the crash call at 03.24 or thereabouts in the early hours of 26 September produced, via the thoracocentesis, approximately 10% of the amount of air that had been aspirated the previous night --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- when [Baby H] had collapsed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Well, we'll come back to this in due course when we come to your opinion. But following that, was [Baby H] kept under fairly close observation? I'm looking at your paragraph 14 now.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you note the fact that there had been contact between the medics at the Countess of Chester and those at the tertiary centre at Arrowe Park?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That is correct, yes. They were clearly very concerned about it, as we have heard earlier in this, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Did you note the fact that -- and if the jury want to find it, it's at tile 399 -- there had been further secretions obtained from the ET tube?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Secretions are a common problem in babies on ventilatory support and, as we have already heard, they can block the ET tube, the endotracheal tube, so she was having secretions around this time.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Was there a further collapse of [Baby H] in the early hours of the 27th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So this is now Sunday, 27 September?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. According to my entry, this collapse occurred at 2.40 am on the 27th and the entry notes -- the medical entry notes there was no explanation for this collapse.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. I think, actually, the evidence was that the collapse had taken place rather earlier than that at about 1 o'clock --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- and that the medical notes had been written up at a later stage.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that is correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Again, and it's recorded at tile 459, was there any obvious explanation for that collapse?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There was no obvious explanation for this. It was unexpected. The notes note, I quote, "no explanation", but the concern was such by this time that they had made arrangements to transfer her to Arrowe Park Hospital.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Given that course of events, did you then go back to the chest X-rays that had been taken of [Baby H]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. There were loads and loads of chest X-rays carried out. We've seen most of them over the last couple of days. What the X-rays show, the early X-rays show a degree of RDS. Then it shows pneumothorax. Then a later X-ray shows what we call the butterfly needle; this is what is used as an emergency to drain air from the pleural space. Following that, she had what we call a pigtail chest drain. It's called a pigtail because it curls within the chest cavity. That was her first, let's call it, proper chest drain.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Following on from that, she had a second -- sorry, that chest drain was placed in her -- what we call the fifth intercostal space, in other words the space between the fifth -- up to the fifth rib. She then had a second chest drain. Now, this was what we call an Argyle chest drain. It's the old-fashioned type.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That is placed lower down in the chest, in the seventh intercostal space.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Just to contextualise that, is that the one that was put in by Dr Jayaram?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct. That's the second drain. That's lower down than most of us would put, but I think it was put further down the chest than ideal because, firstly, the ideal place is the fifth intercostal space. Well, there was a chest drain in there already.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The needle aspiration -- this is another needle aspiration -was carried out lower down the chest.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That's visible on one of the X-rays. So the chest drain, this Argyle chest drain, was inserted lower down the chest and it led to a significant improvement. Her oxygen requirements fell and she stabilised. So that was the second chest drain.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If we follow things sequentially by looking at the chest X-rays, there was a further deterioration caused by another accumulation of air in the pleural space and this led to her third chest Xray and this was the one inserted by Dr Gibbs. This was the third chest drain, I should say, not chest X-ray. This was the
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: third chest drain that was inserted and this was her second pigtail.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So at this time she had three chest drains and this was inserted slightly above chest drain 1. So on this occasion -- and again, following the insertion of the third chest drain, her condition again improved and her oxygen requirements reduced to 30% according to Dr Gibbs' notes. In other words, these chest drains were lifesavers.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you then, having gone through the chest X-rays, review the nursing notes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And did you move from the nursing notes to the notes made by the staff at Arrowe Park once [Baby H] had been transported and taken to there?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. So having reviewed all that material, I want to turn, if I may, to the observations section of your report, which is paragraph 28 and onwards.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You've already told us that [Baby H] had RDS.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I think you've told us that her symptoms were consistent with that particular condition.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Was the treatment that she was given acceptable or not so far as your point of view is concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Starting off with CPAP and additional oxygen was correct. When her condition worsened, placing her on ventilatory support was correct. A couple of hours later she was given surfactant. That was correct. She was clearly unwell. They picked up the fact that she had a pneumothorax and they put a chest drain in the right -- in the ideal place, in the fifth intercostal space. That was correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Her condition was pretty unstable, though, despite all of this, which is why she ended up with three chest drains on the left side of her chest. It's very, very unusual for a baby to require three chest drains, but if needs must then that is what you should do. So therefore, the first -- the problem with a chest drain is this: that when there is air in the pleural space you
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: will see a pattern where the chest drain is noted to be -- "swinging" was the word used.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That means that the holes at the end of the chest drain are patent, they're open, and therefore air is being taken out of the space, this pleural space, and is not going back in. So if the chest drain is connected to a flutter valve, the flutter valve will flutter. If the chest drain is connected to what we call an underwater seal then you'll see the water in the tube moving up and down, ie it is swinging. That's fine and that tells you that you've inserted the chest drain and it's functioning.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The problem is this: once the lung is fully expanded there is no pleural space and therefore the chest drain will stop swinging because the lung, the surface of the lung, is full up against the chest drain. But the chest drain may also stop swinging because it's in the wrong place or not so much in the wrong place, there is air accumulating somewhere else in the lung. That's difficult and the only way to distinguish the cause of the chest drain not swinging is to do another chest X-ray and/or transilluminate the chest.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Transillumination, of course, you can do there and then. Doing a chest X-ray takes time because you've got to get the radiographer to the unit, take the photo and so on.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, managing a pneumothorax is difficult, you know. It's a difficult condition to manage and on the whole you have to rely on the well-being of the baby. If you have inserted a chest drain and the baby is improving then you know your treatment has worked.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If the baby's condition deteriorates then that is as a result of either the pneumothorax is recurring or the chest drain is blocked or both.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Therefore it's quite -- it's a difficult condition to manage and they managed it -- I think they managed it very satisfactorily.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Okay. So far as the pneumothorax or pneumothoraces were concerned, were they or were they not a consequence of the RDS?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think they were a consequence of the RDS. I think the original pneumothorax was a complication of the RDS.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's a well-known complication of RDS.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But turning to the collapses, the two collapses that required the use of adrenaline and CPR, were they -- let's deal with them one by one. Was the collapse requiring the use of adrenaline in the early hours of 26 September the consequence of a pneumothorax?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, because the pneumothorax had been treated at that time.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What about the collapse in the early hours of the 27th, the following night?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, the same. The pneumothorax had been treated by that time, at that time, so therefore you cannot explain the collapse on the basis of the pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We've heard from the treating doctors that they were unable to explain these two collapses. Is there an alternative reasonable explanation in your view for the collapses?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. On one occasion there was a blocked tube, but there was no blocked tube during this collapse. And in my report I have gone as far as to say that the pneumothorax -- sorry, that the collapses cannot be the -- sorry, I will start again. That the collapse was not the result of a pneumothorax because the pneumothorax had been treated.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Infection is another option.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There's little evidence of infection.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We've heard of a raised CRP level.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The CRP level was 50-something, I think, which is a marker of inflammation and infection, but she was -- firstly, she was on antibiotics and to fast-forward a bit, once she went to Arrowe Park they did a lumbar puncture, which was normal, so no evidence of meningitis, and also once she got to Arrowe Park her condition recovered, therefore I would not expect infection -- her pattern of collapse is not what one finds in a baby whose deterioration is the result of infection.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You've dealt with that particular issue in the context of other cases from time to time --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- as we've got to this stage of the case. But perhaps you can deal with it by answering what I hope is a straightforward question, which is: if this collapse was due to infection, would you expect [Baby H] to have collapsed in the way she collapsed in the early hours of either the 26th or 27 September?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, none at all. Her deterioration would have been far more gradual and, as we've discussed in previous cases, I would have expected other features, clinical features of infection, to have shown up, and this was not the case. So with infection you do not suddenly go from baby stable, chest drain or chest drains in place, and suddenly there's this crash with a huge drop in heart rate and a drop in oxygen saturation occurring very, very quickly and also requiring such intense resuscitation. You know, adrenaline, atropine. These drugs are not used -- they're required but they are not used that commonly in neonatal units and I think, as Dr Gibbs said that, so she was resuscitated very effectively, I must say, but she would not have required this degree of resuscitation if the problem was a developing infection.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Sorry, yes. You're quite right. What in your view was the cause of the pneumothorax or the pneumothoraces in [Baby H]'s case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The fact that she had respiratory distress syndrome and that she had been -- although she'd been treated for that, she received surfactant relatively late, but the underlying cause was the respiratory distress syndrome.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What was your view as to the delay, if there was a delay, in administering surfactant to [Baby H]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm unclear as to the policy at the Countess of Chester Hospital, but in Dr Gibbs' evidence he suggested that they were waiting for a chest X-ray to ensure that the position of the breathing tube, the endotracheal tube, was in a satisfactory position before giving the surfactant. That is important because if the tip of the tube is in one lung, and it generally goes into the right lung if it's too long, if it goes into the right lung and you then give surfactant without knowing where the tip
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: of that endotracheal tube is, your dose of surfactant would go down into the right lung and none would go into the left lung, and that can cause significant complications.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So in some units, and the Countess of Chester may be one, it's commonplace to wait for the chest X-ray to make sure that the tip of the endotracheal tube is in a satisfactory position so that when you give the surfactant, it goes into both lungs. Most other hospitals now don't wait for a chest X-ray and you insert an endotracheal tube, listen with a stethoscope to ensure that you can hear air entry on both sides, and if you can, will administer surfactant as soon as possible. But the delay may have been because they were following their own protocol at that hospital at that time.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. So going back to your report then, please, and looking at -- I just want to -- I think we just dealt with the surfactant issue, which is paragraph 3.24.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you take the view, looking at your paragraph 3.25, that the surfactant was late or that it was not late in effect?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And what consequence is that likely to have had so far as [Baby H] was concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, surfactant reduces the stiffness in the lungs that babies have when they have respiratory distress syndrome. If your lungs are stiff and you are mechanically ventilated or if you are struggling to breathe, you are more likely to develop a pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So if the surfactant had been given sooner, it reduced but didn't remove, but it reduced the likelihood of developing a pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Having reviewed the records, did you reach a view as to the stage by which it was likely that [Baby H] had developed her first pneumothorax? I'm looking at your paragraph 3.26.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I wrote it down. I think in my view [Baby H] developed a pneumothorax by around 06.00 hours on 24 September.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What effect would the fact that she was on mechanical ventilation have had on that particular circumstance?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If you're ventilated and you develop a pneumothorax, it's likely to exacerbate or make that pneumothorax worse, just
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: because you're putting pressure into the lungs at a higher pressure than a baby would achieve if they were breathing spontaneously. So you are going to make that air leak worse.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Moving on to your 3.29, a treatment was given for that first pneumothorax; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: An emergency intervention was given, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. What was that intervention, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's called a thoracocentesis and in essence it's using a small needle, which is inserted into the -- through a space between the ribs into the chest and air is aspirated out of that, usually by putting the -- the device is called a butterfly, it has a needle and small tube on the end of that. The needle is put into the chest. If there is air in the chest when the other end of the device is put under water it bubbles, so you can either allow it to bubble out or, as I think in this case, someone put a syringe on the end and actually aspirated air out and measured air out.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What should happen to that needle once that exercise has been undertaken?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The purpose of doing an emergency thoracocentesis is to relieve the tension in the air leak because that's the lifethreatening -- it's a life-threatening condition.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So that is a very temporary solution. You take some of the air — you don't need it take all of the air, you just need to relieve the tension, and the second part is that this should be followed up by a formal chest drain insertion. But what should happen, once you've removed the air or released the tension, is that that needle should be taken from the chest because when you remove the tension, the lung will re-expand and there's a risk that the lung tissue will then abut the sharp edge of the needle as the lung re-expands. So once you've undertaken your emergency measure, you should remove the needle, then do your chest X-ray, or insert your formal drain and then do your chest X-ray, depending on the clinical condition of the baby.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And is that what happened?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. There appears to have been an acute deterioration at that time with [Baby H], a clinical deterioration. blocks.text: Now, just taking a step back at that stage and considering the issue of the pneumothorax or pneumothoraces that had manifested themselves up to that point, did you reach a view as to what the likely cause of that or those was?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The pneumothoraces, I think, were caused by her respiratory distress syndrome.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In that context what did the lack of an early administration of surfactant have?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, it would have exacerbated/increased the risk of pneumothoraces developing, because the lungs would have remained stiff for the period that she had not received the surfactant therapy.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And did the breathing support, in whatever form it had taken up to that stage, have a part to play?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, any respiratory support, be it CPAP, but more importantly if a baby's placed on a ventilator, that will also increase the risk of a pneumothorax. So [Baby H] unfortunately had a number of factors which made her chances of developing pneumothorax higher than that of another baby.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think you've already told us that the butterfly needle had been left in as well --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- with the associated risk. One of the questions that we dealt with earlier was the issue of three chest drains. Did you consider that in the context of [Baby H]'s clinical presentation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Currently, with the advent of antenatal steroids and surfactant therapy, it's very unusual for babies to need three chest drains on the same side. Years ago, and certainly when I trained, antenatal steroids weren't given to mums and surfactant hadn't been invented then, so babies had very stiff lungs and it was not uncommon for babies to have as many as five chest drains. Those days are long gone, thankfully, and therefore it's now very uncommon for babies to have three chest drains in situ, particularly in one lung.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as the -- I'm looking at your paragraph 3.41 now.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: One of the issues that was explored with the treating medics was the precise place at which drains were inserted. Can you help us with that in the context of the problems as [Baby H] was presenting at the time?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: As I alluded to, years ago it was common for babies to have lots of chest drains. Although there was an optimum position for you to place the drain, if babies need multiple drains you clearly can't put all of those drains in the optimal position. Now doctors rarely have to insert chest drains and it's now recommended that the drain, chest drain, is put in at the side of the chest rather than at the front of the chest, just by the armpit, and it's recommended that you count down the ribs and place the drain in the fourth or fifth space between the ribs.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Sometimes counting that can be quite difficult in a baby, it's much easier in an adult. So if you were just inserting one
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: drain, you would insert it at the side and you would place it in the fourth or fifth space between the ribs. Clearly, once you have got one drain in, you can't place the second drain in that position, so you have to place it somewhere else, and the -- and the choice is down to the clinician. But what is difficult in treating pneumothoraces is that, unlike in adults who have a chest drain, which is placed when they are sitting up, babies who are ill are lying down and so the air rises and so the air of the pneumothorax rises.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: When you put the chest drain in horizontally, these tubes are very and it's quite difficult to angle them upwards to come into contact with that pocket of air if you're placing the drain in from the side of the chest.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So an alternative way of dealing with that is to place a chest drain at the front of the chest. That goes in a slightly different position, it goes in a different rib space, but is associated (a) with more complications, in that there are major vessels just underneath where you're planning to put an anterior chest drain, and (b) it causes -- all chest drains cause some scarring but it causes scarring and in a female there's a risk of it interfering with breast tissue. So it is not without its risk. As a life-saving measure of course you would do it, but there are more complications, and it would have been my own choice to have put anterior chest drain in, but I'm mindful of the fact that doctors probably now haven't been taught that technique and therefore would choose another rib space to put a lateral drain in.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Okay. So there you are in effect assessing the drain put in by Dr Jayaram; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I mean, Dr Jayaram, I heard his evidence, he undertook a life-saving measure, he explained that he couldn't put a drain in the fifth intercostal space because there was already a drain there. He chose a rib space two below that. And he was under a lot of stress at the time. This was a life-saving procedure and he did it to save a life, and I think that was the right thing for him, particularly if he is not competent or hadn't thought of putting an anterior chest drain in.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He may never have done that and in the heat of that moment I would have expected him to do something he was competent to do.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dealing with -- I'm turning to your paragraph 3.42 and the various deteriorations of [Baby H]. You deal there with the position immediately after Dr Harkness had put in the pigtail drain, the first drain.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That [Baby H] had stabilised, but that early on the morning of the 25th, so we're still before either of the counts in this case, but early on the morning of the 25th there was an acute deterioration. Can you tell us what conclusions you drew so far as that was concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, what was noted was that the drain was -- I'll go back.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: When a drain is inserted there are two ways you can allow the air to come out. The best way really is to attach the end of a drain and put it to an underwater seal, which the second drain — that was the method used in the second drain.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In the first drain they used something called a flutter valve or a Heimlich valve which is not as effective at draining the air but is a recognised method. [Baby H] had a flutter valve attached to the end of the pigtail and at some point the flutter valve stopped fluttering, stopped moving. So that meant either the drain had become dislodged or had been blocked in some way which meant that there was no fluttering. If that happens then air -- if there's still a hole in the lung, air will reaccumulate and the child will clinically deteriorate.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: At that stage was a butterfly needle used to perform a thoracocentesis?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, at that stage there was another thoracocentesis and 70ml of air was aspirated using a butterfly.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And despite that fact, shortly afterwards -- and it's at tile 48 should anyone want to look at it -- was there a chest X-ray which showed the presence of a large pneumothorax?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is that followed by a second thoracocentesis?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think a third. I think there was another one with 60ml and there was a third one that yielded no air at all.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And that's when the chest drain number 2 was inserted by Dr Jayaram.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. The X-ray that corresponds to that time is the one taken at 2.29, which is tile 55?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You've already dealt with the positioning of that. Is there any issue so far as the timing of the second chest drain was concerned so far as your opinion is concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, there is. There was a second -- there was a thoracocentesis, in which 70ml of air was aspirated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There was then a chest X-ray and then a second and then a third thoracocentesis. So a long time elapsed between doing the emergency intervention of the thoracocentesis and the formal insertion of the chest drain by Dr Jayaram. It may have been that the doctor present was unable to insert a formal chest drain and that may have been why [Baby H] had multiple thoracocenteses. But that wouldn't be a usual -- that wouldn't be usual practice. Usual practice is to aspirate the air to remove the tension and then follow that up immediately by inserting a drain, not having repeated thoracocenteses or waiting for an X-ray.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. Just taking a step back and looking at [Baby H]'s deterioration in the early hours of the 25th, did you reach a conclusion as to what the likely cause of her deterioration was?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think that deterioration was a re-accumulation of the pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No. Once the chest drain was placed, she stabilised.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What was clear is by about 2.15 that morning, the drains were not fluttering in the case of the pigtail catheter or the fluid wasn't swinging in the underwater seal in the case of the more traditional catheter.

blocks.text: So it would appear that both drains were blocked and that -there was a further accumulation of air, which caused her to clinically deteriorate. A consultant was called in again and there was a third chest drain put in, which was a second

blocks.text: pigtail. So by this point she had two pigtail catheters and a third chest drain and --
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Just trying to put that into context of the evidence that we heard. This is Dr Gibbs' --

blocks.text: I beg your pardon, yes.

blocks.text: Not at all.

So by this time [Baby H] had three chest drains in situ. The insertion of that third drain was successful as the oxygen requirement immediately reduced.

blocks.text: Yes. There was a much more serious desaturation later that morning at 03.22 hours. I'm afraid I'm jumping about a bit in your reports because it's necessary to do that in order to keep the sequence so far as the chronology of the events is concerned.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Was there a difference between what had happened up to that stage and what happened at about 03.20 on the morning of 26 September?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, these events were different. The similarities were that there was a profound desaturation, bradycardia and poor colour, but with this event, around 03.24, when the clinical team listened to the chest they could hear air entry and it appeared to be equal on both sides, which is not what they found when there was re-accumulation of air, and also they could see chest wall movement. So when the ventilator was breathing in they could see the chest rising and when the ventilator was breathing out they could see the chest falling.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That was not the case when either there was a re-accumulation of air or if the chest drains were blocked, and in addition they could see that the chest drains were patent and they could see some fluid coming out of the drains.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Okay. Just trying to understand what you've just told us, the collapse at 03.24 or thereabouts, when the medical practitioners listened to either side of [Baby H]'s chest, they could actually hear air going in and out?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So what does that tell us so far as whether or not there's a collapsed lung, a pneumothorax?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If there's a collapsed lung, the air entry would be unequal in that you would hear air going into the normal lung but you would have reduced air entry and you wouldn't hear breath sounds on the side where the lung was collapsed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So the previous collapses had been associated with a collapsed left lung?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Therefore you wouldn't hear air going in?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Therefore you have tension or pressure from the air between the outside of the lung and the inside of the chest?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Therefore you don't hear any air or a reduced amount of air going into that side?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But what was happening at 03.24 or thereabouts was different?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It was different. They could hear air going into both sides of the chest. Of course it also means that the endotracheal tube was not blocked, whereas in some of the previous problems they could not hear air entry on either side of the chest because the endotracheal tube was blocked. So this event tells me that the endotracheal tube was not blocked and that there was no re-accumulation of air.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What about the consequences, the real world consequences for [Baby H]? Other than unblocking a tube and/or re-inflating a lung or deflating the tension pneumothorax, what were the consequences for [Baby H] of this particular collapse that differentiated it from what had gone before?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the other collapses there appeared to be an obvious cause, either a blocked tube or a re-accumulation of air, and the clinical deterioration was rectified by intervention by the medical staff. Once the endotracheal tube was unblocked or once
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: the air leak was drained, [Baby H] recovered. This was very different in that [Baby H] went on to have a cardiac arrest and the interventions provided by the medical staff did not rectify the situation for some time. She required chest compressions, adrenaline and atropine, and that went on for some 20 minutes or so.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So would it be fair or unfair to say that this event has very different characteristics to what preceded it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This event has very different characteristics. I can find no obvious clinical or mechanical cause to account for this collapse or to account for why [Baby H] did not recover as she had done with what was routine intervention.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Moving on to events of the following early morning, if we may, so we're going on to the early hours of the 27th, Sunday, 27 September. We know that [Baby H] collapsed at or about 00.55 that morning.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. This collapse again was heralded with a bradycardia and desaturation. The medical team listened to the chest and could hear air entry. They've bagged using the Neopuff through the endotracheal tube.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They also performed suction on the endotracheal tube because [Baby H] had previously had a blocked tube and there had been secretions, so they, as a precautionary thing, they sucked out that tube. And yet she still did not improve. Then as a result they electively removed the ET tube because of the previous history that her tubes had been blocked. I couldn't find any comment as to whether this tube was blocked or not, but it was a reasonable thing to do in the circumstances.

She then was re-intubated but that did not improve the situation and again her heart rate remained seriously low. blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think if we look at what Nurse Tomlins has noted -- and I'm afraid I'm going from my notes now so I'll just have to check first of all...
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Pause)
I think there is something in here about whether or not there was anything in the tube, but I think it's...
It relates to 00.55, so we're going to have to scroll down a bit. There we are at the bottom:
"Profound desaturation to 40% despite equal bilateral air entry and positive capnography. ET suction yielded nil secretions."
So it may be that that informs the position, does it or not?
It doesn't tell us whether the tube was blocked or not, but it does indicate that -- if the tube is blocked you wouldn't get any secretions if you suction, so I don't think that helps us either way.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No, all right. Thank you. What view did you take of this particular collapse, please, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, again, it mirrored the previous collapse that we've just spoken about in that although there was a bradycardia and a desaturation, there was no obvious cause to account for that and no cause as to why [Baby H] did not improve with routine measures. So whether the tube was blocked or not, they took the tube out and bagged her. So you would have expected her to improve.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There had not been a re-accumulation of the air leak, but even going back prior to that, when the staff listened in they could hear air entry on both sides of the chest and the capnography, the CO2 detector at the end of the endotracheal tube, was positive, showing that carbon dioxide was coming out of the chest. So that would indicate actually that the tube was not blocked.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Thank you. Can we deal with a slightly different issue, which has been explored with some of the witnesses as we've heard the evidence from the treating medical practitioners, and I think you deal with it in your statement of 26 September 2022. It's your page 4 of 6. It's my Lord's page 5520 and it's paragraph 2.7, please, Dr Bohin. It concerns the movement or non-movement of the non-pigtail drain, so the Dr
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Jayaram drain, if I can call it that. It may be a name that brings it more to mind.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were you asked to consider whether or not in your view there was evidence to either support or rebut a theory that in some way the movement of the tip of that drain had interfered either with the heart or the vagal nerve or some other structure within the body that would account for [Baby H]'s two collapses, the first in the early hours of the 26th and the second in the early hours of the 27th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I was asked to comment on that. What's clear is that if the tip of a drain is abutting structures in the centre of the chest, ie the heart or nerves in the chest, that can cause — although I have to say I have never seen it, but in theory that can cause a bradycardia, ie a fall in heart rate, and a clinical deterioration.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But although it's clear that the Dr Jayaram drain had moved on a sequence of X-rays, it didn't move after the X-ray on 26 September. The subsequent X-rays show that it's in the same position. Therefore I don't think that that drain can be the cause for [Baby H]'s deterioration with the theory offered that it may have been pressing on the heart or other vital structures and causing the collapse.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It may be obvious from what you've said, but why not?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because it wasn't in the position -- it wasn't moving then. It had been secured by Dr Gibbs. It had moved before, the treating clinicians told us that, and the X-ray shows that the tip is in a different position.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But once it had been secured, it didn't move and wasn't touching the heart.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, and yet we --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And yet [Baby H] collapsed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In the same way on the 27th as she did on the 26th; is that what you're saying?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So does it follow that because it didn't move and because therefore it can't have been responsible for the collapse on the 27th and because the collapse on the 26th was very similar to the 27th, you have taken a view that it can't be responsible for either?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The X-ray taken on the 26th was at 2.30 and [Baby H] collapsed at 3.24. So the X-ray showed that the tube was in a position not touching the heart, and so both the collapses occurred after we know the position of that tube was not next to the heart.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Those are all the questions I have for you at this stage. I'm sure Mr Myers has some questions.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Bohin, with regard to the event on 26 September at about 3.20 in the morning, so event number 1, you haven't identified any cause to account for that, have you?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And with regard to the second event, that at about 00.55 on the morning of 27 September, again you haven't identified any cause for that, have you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm going to go through the events, if you would assist me with this, just identifying various items we've looked at, just to get things in sequence and deal with what you have told us in your evidence, so I'd be grateful for your help there.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The first point I would like to deal with this is: do you agree that the delivery of surfactant was late?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Looking in the first report you wrote at paragraph 7.6, just as to the potential effect of it coming late, you say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "The delay is probably significant as surfactant therapy improves lung compliance and reduces stiffness in the lungs, making ventilation easier and the therapy works in minutes."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Certainly there's a delay of up to 36 hours post-birth with this, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, there is, but you would not normally give surfactant at birth in a baby of this gestation, but you would give
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: surfactant as soon as you had made the diagnosis of respiratory distress syndrome.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. And it's well-known, isn't it, that early or appropriately timed doses of surfactant can reduce the risk of pneumothorax, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We know that a little after 7 o'clock on the morning of 24 September 2015, there was a desaturation that went down to the 50s? In fact, it will help if I do show some of the slides with this on so we can follow it.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mr Murphy, could you put up T5, please? Can we scroll down a little bit further, please?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we continue down, we're going down to the 24th if we could, please. Just to the bottom of this page.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This is an entry -- we saw it with Dr Ventress.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's made at 8.20 in the morning on 24 September, but we can see it refers to that [Baby H] had been fine in the night, it refers to the 6 am cares, and it says that she's since deteriorated and had a profound desaturation down to the 50s. Do you see that, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So that's some time maybe just after 7 o'clock or thereabouts on 24 September. Now, as it happens, there had been a delay in intubation, hadn't there, round about this time, do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't know there'd been a delay in intubation. The SHO arrived -- this is written at 8.20. The desaturation occurred -we don't exactly know when -- around 7 o'clock. And then she was intubated by the SHO at 8, I think.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. If we scroll up, please, and go back. We can see:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Intubated on first attempt at 8.10."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The requirement for that having been identified round about 6 o'clock, in fact. Scroll back up, please, a little bit higher. Pausing there, please. We can see at the bottom of this note --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "May need intubation if not improved."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Do you see that, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but she had improved overnight and was in air so the team wouldn't have wanted to intubate her overnight.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And when she desaturated that morning, things had changed, and therefore there was a need to intubate then, but overnight she didn't need intubating and in fact she was in air, so she was fine.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If you look in your first report at paragraph 7.4, Dr Bohin, you say this, talking about this period:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "[Baby H] continued to deteriorate. A decision was made to intubate and ventilate at 06.00 on 24 September 2015 when she was said to be gasping."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "There was a delay and this was not carried out until 07.45, which in my view is not acceptable practice."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So when I asked you whether it was a delay in this way and it was unacceptable, that comes from your report, Dr Bohin.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I must say, I understood your question to be from earlier, from the previous night, you were saying it's a much longer delay than that 1 and three-quarter hours between that time. But that was -- maybe I misunderstood -- because I don't know whether that was the reason. Anyway, she accepts there was a delay.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I accept there was a delay.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's why I went through those notes, my Lord, to identify the exact time and where it was said at 6 o'clock there may need to be intubation.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: To be quite clear, Dr Bohin, in your report, do you agree, that was an unacceptable delay in intubation?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, there was a delay.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: As for the pneumothorax that developed in [Baby H], your opinion is that she had almost certainly developed it by maybe about 6 o'clock on the 24th; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Your opinion is that that pneumothorax is likely to be a consequence of her clinical condition, which was RDS, respiratory distress syndrome?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And also late provision of surfactant will have made that worse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Looking at paragraph 7.9 of the same report, Dr Bohin, it's your opinion that:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "The air leak was probably small prior to this intubation but it increased after intubation with ventilation."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, because we know that ventilation exacerbates air leak.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. So we have the late delivery of surfactant, followed by delayed ventilation, but when the ventilation takes place, that may have made the air leak worse; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is, but they had to ventilate her.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So the treatment probably did make the air leak worse but there was no option but to intervene to ventilate her.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was a life-saving measure.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that should have happened sooner, shouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It should have happened sooner, yes. But if it had happened sooner, the air leak still would have been exacerbated by ventilation regardless of what time she was ventilated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we move forwards now to 10.05 -- sorry, 8.35 on 24 September 2015, and we put up -- look in your second report at paragraph 6.8, please.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, which?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Your first report at paragraph 6.8, Dr Bohin. My mistake, you first report at paragraph 6.8.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We're moving forward to 8.35 in the morning, still on the 24th --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- and there was a desaturation with [Baby H] down to 54%; that's correct, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It's at this time, isn't it, that there was a positive cold light examination on the left side of the chest and a chest X-ray was ordered?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Keeping in mind the timings, she was now being ventilated, wasn't she, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The chest X-ray was now ordered, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But surfactant had yet to be given, it wasn't actually given until shortly before midday, was it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The whole point of surfactant is to keep -- assist with the lungs being pliable so they can move more easily during respiration, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we move forwards to about 10.05 on 24 September and paragraph 6.9 of your first report, Dr Bohin. 6.10.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Are you with me, paragraph 6.10?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: At 10.05, there is a further deterioration whilst on the ventilator, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And this is the point at which the first butterfly needle is inserted into [Baby H]'s chest, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You've looked at the X-rays and looked at what happened with this first butterfly needle, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm going now to look at what you say about that in your report. My Lord, it's the second report -- I apologise that we move between them, but the findings are (inaudible) critically because you are looking at different things at different times, Dr Bohin, going across different reports.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Could you go to paragraph 3.13 in your second report? That butterfly needle is introduced shortly after 10 o'clock or thereabouts; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: A butterfly needle, as you've explained to us, should be removed as soon as possible, shouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It has a sharp tip that can tear delicate lung tissue if it's left in situ as the lung expands; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It went in shortly after 10 o'clock. Could we put up the radiograph, please, Mr Murphy, at 12658, which shows us the situation at 11.24? So a little under an hour and a half later, an hour and 20 minutes later.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Pause there, thank you, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We can see the timing of that was 11.24 on 24 September. We can see that even at this time it appears that butterfly needle is still in situ, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's the white line with the point at the top. It's the right of our picture but towards the top of [Baby H]'s left lung?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Your views as to the leaving of butterfly needles you express in paragraph 3.38 in that second report --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- where you say that leaving the needle in the chest is dangerous if the lung expands for the reasons you've already explained to us --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- and it's not currently recommended.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And your concern as to that in this situation, Dr Bohin — I'm looking at paragraph 3.44 in the same report -- your concern was that leaving the butterfly needles or needle in the chest for prolonged periods may have punctured lung tissue and contributed to the subsequent pneumothoraces; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it may have done.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In the same paragraph you say that:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Had [Baby H] been given earlier and multiple doses of surfactant and was better sedated and paralysed, she would have been easier to ventilate with lower pressures and at less risk of accumulation."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Leaving a butterfly needle in situ like that is, I'm going to put it this way, sub-optimal practice, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, because it's hazardous.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Moving to the next event I'd ask to look at with you, please, Dr Bohin. If we put up tile 41, please, Mr Murphy, we're moving to 8.50 on the evening of 24 September. If we just go behind that tile 41.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I hope I've got the correct reference myself.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we go to the left-hand side, at the top, please, we've got the entry by Ms Letby at 22.34. Can you see that at the top left-hand entry?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Desaturation to 40% at 20.50."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see that? Sorry to go straight into the centre of there but I'm going to go directly to the point.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I can.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: When you came to consider that in your report, Dr Bohin, at paragraph 31 --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: My second report? Paragraph 3.31?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Give me one moment, please. Yes. Perhaps look at paragraph 3.30, just to read yourself in. You point out that after the 20.50 desaturation, the dose of morphine and the ventilator settings needed to be increased --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- which indicates that [Baby H] was struggling and is an indication the air had re-accumulated and you say that wasn't recognised at the time.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it doesn't appear to be.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The significance of that, Dr Bohin, is that if [Baby H] had been sedated in the way that would have been optimal, her muscles would have been relaxed and she wouldn't have been struggling against the ventilator; do you agree with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She may not have been, but it's -- recurrent pneumothoraces are very difficult to treat. So you need to do everything possible to try and reduce the risk of air reaccumulating and one of those things is to obviously keep babies settled so they are not breathing against the ventilator. But sometimes, even despite that, because of the poor compliance of the lungs, pneumothoraces will still re-accumulate. So yes, it may mitigate it but it doesn't necessarily completely remove the risk of it.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You pointed out in your evidence earlier that there is no X-ray taken, I think it was between -- was it 11.24 in the morning of the 24th until 01.40 on the morning of the 25th?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: This occurs during that period, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And it may be thought that with a baby in a condition that [Baby H] was in perhaps rather closer monitoring with the radiographs or X-rays may have assisted to see what was happening in her chest with her lungs.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The X-ray would have helped but you really need to go on clinical findings as well. So an X-ray undoubtedly would have helped but so would just clinical observation, really.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. In any event it would have been better if she had been sedated and the muscles relaxed so she wasn't struggling against the ventilation, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm unsure of the policy at the Countess of Chester regarding muscle relaxing babies. It tends to be used less often now but in any case adequate sedation should stop movement, whether you use a muscle relaxant or not, and I think she would have been better placed to have had more sedation, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm going to move next to tile 44, please, which takes us forward to the period between 1.15 and 1.25 on 25 September. So this is several hours after what we've just looked at there. Tile 44, please, Mr Murphy. I'm also looking at your report 2, paragraph 3.32, Dr Bohin.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we just scroll down, please, Mr Murphy, we're going to move to an entry that starts at 01.14 on the 25th.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can we see where the entry begins, Mr Murphy, just so everyone can remember this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's an entry by Dr Ventress. We have looked at this. 25 September 2015. The entry was made at 3.30 in the morning. I'm just going to remind us about the extent of the desaturation. Can we see at 01.14, it describes being bleeped.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we continue down over the page, we can stop there, thank you. We can see at 01.25 now a profound desaturation down to the 30s. Do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In your report at paragraph 3.32, Dr Bohin, you refer to this and you say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "The pigtail was no longer fluttering, meaning it was either blocked or had become dislodged."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "The lack of fluttering should have alerted staff that, for whatever reason, the drain was not functioning properly and the lack of fluttering should merit a medical review before a clinical collapse."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Still on the same note, but seeing how [Baby H] proceeded, if we carry on down to 01.45, towards the bottom of that page, [Baby H] desaturates again, doesn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, because she's got a re-accumulation of her air leak.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. If we continue down, please, to the entry at 02.40, is she down to 80% saturation at this point? It says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "ETT removed as sats 80%."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So in effect that is a desaturation down to 80%, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, her saturations are reduced because the tube's blocked.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, that's where I'm going. So we find there's a blocked tube at this point after there'd been a further desaturation at 02.40?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we move, please, to -- continue down, we can see we've got 03.00, a further profound desaturation to 26% now.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Which is a very significant desaturation, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, because she's got a tension pneumothorax by this stage.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And this is the point at which the next chest drain, or round about this point, soon afterwards, when the next chest drain is inserted, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Now, you explained earlier on, when you were giving evidence, there's a delay between the thoracocentesis at 03.00 —
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- and the chest drain being put in a little bit later, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. I can't see when the chest drain was actually put in by Dr Jayaram.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we scroll down, or if it's not here we can go to page T59 -- can we go to tile 59, please, Mr Murphy?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Tile 51 first, I apologise. Tile 51. We can see Dr Jayaram's handwriting appear in the note timed at 04.55 down in the centre of the page. Can you see that, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He charts what happened after his arrival at about 01.50.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we scroll down, please. We need to go to the next page, tile 59, please. If we go down towards the foot of this page we can see it -- can you go up a little bit, please?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It doesn't say the actual time though.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No, the note says it's made at about 04.40. It doesn't give an exact time, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We'll see a radiograph shortly. Your observation on this, Dr Bohin, was that we've seen over the period that Dr Jayaram attended and over this incident, there were two occasions when needles were inserted to aspirate the chest, weren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you made the observation in your evidence that it would have been better to proceed to inserting the second chest drain sooner than actually happened, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, prior to the -- immediately after the thoracocentesis, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, immediately after the first one?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: So the film's rotated, so I'm afraid if you want precise detail on the tip of the non-pigtail catheter, you would need to ask a radiologist because, to me, the rotation means that I can't interpret that.
